title: Gabriel Jesus: what Manchester City can expect from ‘the new Neymar’
trail: The 19-year-old striker is explosive, bold, possesses mesmerising skills and will not be fazed by the Premier League’s physicality or intensity. But history shows that signing Brazilians comes with no guarantees
body: In the summer of 1987, Francisco Ernami Lima de Silva scored against England in a friendly and shortly afterwards left Palmeiras for Newcastle United. The deal was brokered by Humberto Silva, a student staying in Worthing to learn English, and Malcolm Macdonald, who knew Peter Beardsley was off to Liverpool. The fee was £575,000 and the player, better known as Mirandinha, became the first Brazilian to play in England. The response was one of innocent ecstasy. “We’ve got Mirandinha, he’s not from Argentina, he’s from Brazil, he’s brill,” went the song, while some fans took to wearing … er … sombreros. Mirandinha’s debut, against Norwich, was a matter of national import, and in his third game, against Manchester United, he scored twice in a 2-2 draw. But, though he finished his first season with a reasonable 12 goals in 29 appearances, he struggled with injury and his unwillingness to pass, juxtaposed against his willingness to shoot from improbable positions, began to grate. At the end of his second season Newcastle were relegated, and Mirandinha went home. It was six years until the next Brazilian arrived in England, and though there has been a continuous flow ever since, Juninho, at Middlesbrough, is perhaps the only unqualified success. So Manchester City’s signing of Gabriel Jesus, Palmeiras’s 19-year-old striker, for an initial £27m comes with no guarantees. But Gabriel Jesus’s pedigree is unarguable. Born in São Paulo, he grew up in the Jardim Peri favela and it was there, playing barefoot on concrete pitches, he developed typically Brazilian skills: he is explosive, inventive and bold, with balance and dexterity verging on the ludicrous. “I’m a fan of Gabriel and I look at him and see myself when I was younger,” none other than Ronaldo told Globo TV. “I see many similarities between us.” There can exist no higher praise, though the media have dubbed him the new Neymar. Also influential in Gabriel Jesus’s development were São Paulo’s notoriously tough amateur leagues, known as the várzea. “They go into tackles to break your leg,” he recalled. But he was not fazed. “Sometimes I’d play as many as three or four matches a day: I couldn’t get enough of it,” he told Fifa’s website. “It’d get to the point when my muscles would cramp up. It’s football. I can’t put my mind to anything else. I’m not interested in hanging out or partying. For me, it’s all about the pitch: training, playing. Even when I go home it’s football the whole time. I think I’m obsessed.” Gabriel Jesus joined Associacao Atlética, an amateur club famed for helping youngsters break into big academies, and after 54 goals in 48 appearances he signed for Palmeiras in July 2013, breaking into the first team in March 2015. Playing as a left-sided attacker, he scored a beauty at Cruzeiro that cemented him in the public consciousness and a few months later won the league’s best newcomer award, before helping Brazil to the final of the Under-20 World Cup. Shortly after the start of the following season, in February 2016, Gabriel Jesus scored for the first time in the São Paulo state championship and 12 days later at River Plate in the Copa Libertadores. In was in March that his career really took off when Alexi “Cuca” Stival became his manager. Appraising a calm, confident finisher not especially suited to defensive work, he moved Gabriel Jesus to centre-forward and was rewarded with another Libertadores goal against Nacional, the eventual champions, then two more away to Rosario Central – though he was sent off for retaliation. He continued through the middle when the Brazilian league began in May and Palmeiras now sit at the top, Gabriel Jesus’s 10 goals in 14 games making him its leading scorer. So it is easy to see why so many top clubs have taken an interest – he is, according to Tim Stillman of the Botafogo Star, “the best young player in South America without a doubt”. It is just as easy to see why he has ended up at City. There are few outstanding centre-forwards in the world and though Sergio Agüero is one, Gabriel Jesus is as similar in style as any substitute or successor could possibly be. He is superb at finding space, both inside the penalty area – he scores a lot of headers for someone who is 5ft 9in – and in behind defences, able to finish calmly and confidently with either foot. “Gabriel, I always say, has not yet reached his peak,” Cuca said recently. “Games teach players new things. Gabriel is taking advantage of opportunities, he knows how to play as a striker, can make diagonal runs, he knows how to come from behind with speed. There are things to improve, but he will be an excellent player.” Which is to say the personal qualities which Pep Guardiola looks for are also present: he is flexible, coachable and decisive. And Guardiola played an important role in ensuring Gabriel Jesus signed for City despite a reported contractual clause stipulating his availability to Manchester United, Bayern Munich, Barcelona, Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain for “just” €24m (£20.3m). Guardiola, though, is said to have bypassed official channels to approach the player personally and the move seems to have been persuasive. Cuca – for it was he who made the claim – immediately qualified it by saying that provided Gabriel Jesus stayed in Brazil until the end of the season, in December, “there’s no problem”. And City have confirmed that to be the plan, though if Palmeiras reach the Libertadores as seems likely, it may be best for his development to see that through too. In the meantime he can enjoy the Olympic football tournament – his developing partnership with the 17-year-old Gabriel “Gabigol” Barbosa looks set to be one of its highlights. With Brazil yet to win a gold in that tournament, there will be significant pressure to succeed, all the more so given their World Cup implosion; Gabriel Jesus has the ability and mentality to deliver. Thanks to Tim Stillman.
